articleTitle: Power/energy: Demand-side load management: The rising cost of peak-demand power means that utilities must encourage customers to manage power usage
abstract: As electricity cost increases, more and more utilities are extending their activities into once-forbidden territory: the customer's side of the meter. In order to increase efficiency and hold the line on costs, they are controlling, directly and indirectly, when and how the electric energy is used - shifting from a supply-side-only viewpoint to demand-side technologies. They are including the customer as a new utility corporate planning option.

articleTitle: Solid state: X-ray lithography breaks the submicrometer barrier; A new X-ray lithography system allowed Bell Labs engineers to make the smallest, fastest MOSFETs yet reported
abstract: Device engineers at Bell Labs have used a new X-ray system to make circuits with MOSFETs that are among the smallest and fastest digital devices ever reported. The MOSFETs have channel lenghts of 0.3 to 0.4 micrometer switching speeds of 30 to 75 picoseconds, and speed-power products of 5 femtojoules (5 × 10-15 Ws) to 50 femtojoules.

The use of computers to control manufacturing has long been routine in continuous-process industries, such as chemicals and oil refining, but only in the past several years has it been introduced in batch-manufacturing industries, such as metal working. The metal-working industries employ by far the largest share of industrial workers in all the advanced countries, and a large percentage of their products are manufactured in medium-sized batches, ranging from hundreds to thousands of products in each batch. It is not feasible to produce such batches by rigid mechanized techniques, like those used in the large-batch automotive industry. To speed medium-range production, the flexibility of computerized automation is needed.

articleTitle: Power/energy: A solar-pond power plant: Israel reviews an experiment which got under way more then a year ago: Will it prove a model for more like it?
abstract: After more than a quarter century of research, Israel has built a 7500-m2 salt pond and turned it into an electric power plant. The experimental 150-kW installation, which began operating in December 1979 in Ein Bokek, near the Dead Sea, collects and stores solar energy in water in which the salt concentration increases with depth. A low-temperature turbogenerator converts the thermal energy into electricity (Fig. 1).

articleTitle: Communications: The crystal detector: By 1920, G.W. Pickard had tested 31 250 possible combinations of materials in search of a practical detector
abstract: We use the term electronics today; in 1906. the term was “radio.” Radio was a new field, and most of the technology had to be developed from scratch. For reliable long-distance communication, sensitive receivers were vitally needed. The heart of the receiver was its detector, the device that demodulated the radio frequency signal and produced an audio frequency current in the headphones that listeners had to wear. Making this detector more sensitive became the goal of every radio engineer. The inventor who did more than any other to develop the crystal detector and turn it into a practical device was an American, Greenleaf Whittier Pickard (1877-1956). Pickard, whose great-uncle was John Greenleaf Whittier, the poet, was born in Portland, Me., and educated at the Lawrence Scientific School, Harvard University, and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. During the Summer of 1899, he received a grant from the Smithsonian Institution to experiment with wireless antennas raised by kites at the Blue Hill Observatory in Milton, Mass. His apparatus was the same as Marconi's (Fig. 1), employing a coherer as the detector, and Pickard soon became aware of its limitation.

articleTitle: Military electronics: EMPs and nuclear power: The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission is studying whether electromagnetic pulses from H-bombs could trigger nuclear plant accidents
abstract: What effects might electromagnetic pulses from exploded nuclear weapos have on nuclear power plants? Might they cause serious accidents in the plants? While preliminary investigations have indicated that such accidents are not likeiy, the Nuciear Regulatory Commission studying the matter to help the U.S. government decide whether new safety requirements are needed at the plants.

articleTitle: The vulnerability of computers: malfunctions may be due to "illegal" operations, to hardware failures, or to combinations of hardware and software failures that simply elude pinpointing
abstract: Digital computers pose unique reliability problems. Serious information-processing errors can occur through one failure lasting a billionth of a second in one of the hundreds of thousands of digital components that switch billions of times a day. Just in the transfer of data between Computers and their peripherals, a million characters may stream toward a printer within 15 minutes, and millions of characters per second flow to and from magnetic-disk memory units. What's more, the tasks that computers generally perform are so complex that some errors can go undetected for long periods of time, until outputs from the machine become sufficiently unreasonable to arouse a user's suspicions. The only way to design reliability into this environment (besides the method of worst-case design that is used in all walks of engineering) is to build various methods into the machine for detecting and correcting malfunctions. Modern computers therefore have complex watchdog hardware and firmware and programs to keep the machines serviceable despite intermittent or continuous hardware failures.

articleTitle: Microprocessors: Design case history: Wang's word processor: A novel distributed-processing design enabled its creators to revolutionize text-handling systems
abstract: Word processors were the up and coming thing in offices when An Wang, founder of Wang Laboratories Inc., in Lowell, Mass., called three of his computer specialists to a secret strategy meeting on Sept. 28, 1975. Dr. Wang was worried because the company's Series 1200 word processor, its initial entry into the market in 1971, was pitted against formidable competition from International Business Machines, Vydec, Burroughs, and Xerox. The Wang word processor had captured perhaps 3 percent of all sales, whereas IBM alone controlled 75 to 80 percent.

articleTitle: Computer: Contiguous-element memories increase storage tenfold: An overlapping-triangle configuration for bubble memories may displace permalloy-chevron types
abstract: A new generation of contiguous-element magnetic-bubble devices can store about 10 times more information than permalloy chevron magnetic-bubble devices and yet be made by standard photolithographic technology. Devices in development have a storage density of 4 million bits per square centimeter. Chevron bubble memories presently offer only about 1 Mb/cm2, and a density of about 1.5 Mb/cm2 may be achieved, but this would strain the capabilities of photolithographic technology. However, a density of 16 Mb/em2 appears within reach with current processing methods for contiguous-disk devices.

articleTitle: Microprocessors: Design case history: Singer's electronic sewing machine: Putting a microprocessor in a sewing machine surprised the skeptics and put its developers for ahead of the competition
abstract: Pressed by a competitor who was selling Japanese manufactured sewing machines for the home at lower cost: the, Singer Sewing Products Group counterattacked. Fer four years, designers and development engineers worked in secret at the Singer headquarters in Elizabeth, N.J., putting together a sewing machine that would, in one stroke, make existing machines on the market obsolete. What they were aiming for was the world's first electronic sewing machine.

articleTitle: Microcomputers: Microprocessors and the M.D.: A new breed of smart medical equipment can diagnose, monitor, analyze, and rehabilitate
abstract: Microprocessor-based electrocardiography instruments are helping combat the No. 1 killer of people in the United States: heart disease. The new ECG instruments not only capture and display real-time and recorded measurements of heart rates, waveforms, and rhythms, but they also process and transfer the data to a remote site for analysis by a cardiologist or a computer. Analysis can point to problems in the electrical conduction networks, heart muscles, valves or blood flow. The latest ECG equipment uses the microprocessor's software-derived intelligence to diagnose some heart defects or to record and warn of abnormal heart rhythms. (See box, p. 49)

Laser radar with higher accuracy and more precise resolution than microwave radar is receiving renewed attention from electronics designers. This interest coincides with the emergence of carbon-dioxide lasers in sman, high-power packages. Once limited to simple applications, such as range finding, or to large, one-of-a-kind uses, such as satellite tracking, laser radars are now being seriously considered for a variety of military and civilian applications including: • Aircraft navigation systems. • Fire-control systems for armored vehicles and aircraft. • Missile guidance. • Line-of-sight command systems for missiles and rockets. • Equipment for research on severe storms. • Instruments for surveying sites for wind turbines. • Clear-air turbulence monitors for aircraft.

articleTitle: Modeling techniques: A repetitive cycle of modeling, testing, and redesign through final production specifications is crucial to eliminating a system's weak links
abstract: The design of a reliable system begins with the earliest feasibility studies and continues through final production blueprints. An initial electronic system design has only 10 to 30 percent of the reliability (mean time between failures — MTBF) of the final product. To increase this, design engineers undertake a repetitive design cycle, modeling reliability, testing predictions in the laboratory, and isolating areas that need improvement and redesigning them. This process is called “reliability growth” and must be carefully planned in order to achieve acceptable reliability by the time the product is ready for production.

articleTitle: Consumer electronics: Wind-induced ions thwart TV reception: High-altitude ionized layers can bounce a signal up to 1500 kilometers outside its normal area of coverage
abstract: If television viewers in Bridgeport, Conn., were suddenly presented with James Garner in "The Rockford Files" from KQTV in St. Joseph, Mo., instead of the customary "News-breakers Reports" on Channel 2 from WCBS-TV in New York they would be startled indeed. Yet such bizarre interference from VHF stations many hundreds of kilometers away does occur occasionally in fringe reception areas all over the U.S.

articleTitle: Power/energy: TMI plus 2: Two years after the ordeal at Three Mile Island, a restructured, safer nuclear industry is envisaged
abstract: March 28, 1979, has become one of those rare days when time seems to divide into two segments: pre-TMI and post-TMI. The events that began on that day at Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania developed into the nation's worst nuclear reactor accident so far, and the trauma has prompted changes in reactor design and the safety strategy of the nuclear power industry.

articleTitle: Education: A crisis in electrical engineering manpower: A review of the problems facing U.S. industry as a result, and a strategy for corrective action
abstract: It is no longer an open question whether the shortage of electrical engineers in the United States is or is not a crisis. It is. Sooner or later every U.S. industry dependent upon electrical engineering will be affected - and there are more such industries now than ever. Toy and automobile manufacturers, even textile and clothing companies, have discovered the value of electronics and computer-based systems in their products or manufacturing processes. Indeed, these new industries, previously unaffected by electrical engineering in any significant way, are the hidden factor that invalidates traditional market surveys of future needs for EEs. It is hard to predict the growing need for electronics specialists in sectors of the economy that never before employed many.

articleTitle: Aerospace: Neutralizing charged-up spacecraft: Electrical charge gathered from space plasma can cause malfunctions or failure, but techniques for minimizing its effects are available
abstract: As early as 1969, telemetered data from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's ATS-5 satellite suggested that the satellite was charging to potentials of more than 10 000 volts relative to the ambient space environment. In 1971, several U.S. Air Force satellites again showed the effects of high surface charges. The symptoms, in all cases: logic circuits switched erratically, sensor signals grew noisy, heat-control mechanisms lost efficiency, and attitude control faltered. The satellites recorded false data and initiated unplanned actions. In 1973, a satellite in the U.S. Defense Communications System actually failed because its power supply malfunctioned.

articleTitle: Communications: Advanced microwave circuits: Computer-aided design and innovative physical configurations help increase performance and reduce costs
abstract: New developments in microwave circuitry are expected to meet future systems requirements for increased RF power, higher frequencies, wider bandwidth, lower noise levels, and smaller highdensity packaging at lower cost. Advanced microwavecircuitryis slated for use in diverse areas such as satellite communications, navigational equipment for ships, radar systems, and phasedarray modules for information transfer systems. (See “Highfrequency components play catch-up,” Spectrum, November 1976, pp. 31-35.)

articleTitle: Power/energy: Reflector satellites for solar power: Solar-cell arrays in arid zones plus microwave transmission to space and back can send power where needed
abstract: As the cost of solar cells drops and their efficiency increases, prospects for a global photovoltaic power system are not beyond the realm of feasibility. In simple terms, such a system would collect the sun's energy at optimum sites around the globe “ sunny, and areas ” and distribute it to buyers anywhere in the world. The system would supply many gigawatts of power continuously without requiring energy storage.

High-definition television, with a much sharper picture than is currently available, is expected to be in retail stores before the decade is out. A number of converging developments are expected to yield a TV picture with over 1100 scanning lines, or roughly twice the number now specified by the three major color television standards in the world. The developments include digital broadcast equipment, wideband analog and digital video tape recorders, direct-broadcast satellites, and TV receivers with large, wide screens.

The changes affect array processors, multiprocessors, and microprogramming that exploit the denser, faster, and cheaper logic and memory circuits provided by LSI. Examples of the influence of LSI are two new supercomputers - the Cyber 205 from the Control Data Corp. and the Burroughs BSP - along with five new mainframes verging on super power: the FPS-164 from Data Point; the Hitachi AS/9000, introduced in the U.S. by National Advanced Systems; the HEP (heterogenous element processor), made by Denelcor; the IBM 3081; and the Amdahl 5860. (The BSP was canceled after this was written, but it is discussed for purposes of comparison.)

articleTitle: Medical electronics: Nuclear medical imaging: Enhanced system designs provide sharper diagnostic images and better biochemical-activity analysis
abstract: New medical imaging systems that blend nuclear detection and computer reconstruction techniques may spare many patients the ordeal of exploratory surgery. The systems employ electronic detectors that can pinpoint atomic particles injected into the body. From information about the site of these particles, numerical computer programs can reconstruct and display three-dimensional representations on a cathode-ray-tube display and can be used to derive information on the biochemical activity of a body area, including organ functions, metabolic rates, and the presence of benign and cancerous tumors.

articleTitle: Computers: Microcomputer standards: Weighing the pros and cons: Standardization of microcomputer hardware and software has been slowed by manufacturers' vested interests
abstract: In the rapidly proliferating world of microcomputers, users are inundated with a welter of competing claims for such things as high-level language capabilities, disk operating systems, assembly-level programming, and bus architectures. With the diversity of the microcomputer field have come the problems of linking the machines together and transferring programs from one make of machine to another. Manufacturers follow the few mainframe standards that are applicable in the area, such as the RS-232-C interface and other so-called standards, such as the Kansas City “standard” for cassette recorders, and now there is a multinational effort under way to formulate a common framework to ease the users' problems while, at the same time, offering manufacturers a common path for the design of peripherals and software.

There was a time when reliable design could be described simply as “picking good parts and using them right.” Nowadays the complexity of systems, particularly electronic systems, and the demand for ultrahigh reliability in many applications means that sophisticated methods based on numerical analysis and probability techniques have been brought to bear, particularly in the early stages of design, on determining the feasibility of systems.

articleTitle: Military: Killer particle beams: Despite continuing research, the feasibility of building particle-beam weapons and the wisdom of using them remain highly uncertain
abstract: The Reagan Administration's announced commitment to more than double military spending in the the next four years has rekindled interest in directed-energy weapons that can expand U.S. military power into outer space. Such weapons would use either laser beams or streams of charged or neutral particles, such as electrons or protons, to shoot down missiles. Though most of the money and effort in directed-energy work is being devoted to developing laser weapons, which are thought to be nearer to realization, the potential vulnerability of lasers to simple counter-measures such as reflective coatings has heightened defense interest in particle-beam weapons. In addition, controversial reports that the Soviet Union is far ahead in the development of such weapons have been used to bolster some military analysts' arguments that a much expanded U.S. effort in beam weapons is required.

articleTitle: Consumer electronics: Projection television: Correcting distortions
abstract: Recent technological advances have sparked renewed interest in projection television systems for the home. Manufacturers are waging a brightness battle, using as their weapons faster optics, higher-gain screens, more efficient phosphors, new picture tube designs, and other innovations. Their objective? Literally to outshine their competitors and win over as many consumers as possible — consumers who may be hard to convince that the big picture is worth the big price.

articleTitle: Best bits: Applications of microprocessors: Mechanics on a chip
abstract: If one can build a computer on a chip, why not nozzles, pumps, valves, and sensors on chips? Hessarchers at Stanford University's Integrated Circuits Laboratory and IBM's San Jose Research Laboratories in California have developed techniques that put devices like these on silicon wafers. The micromechanical structures are fabricated in much the same way as conventional ICs.

articleTitle: The elusiveness of software: In the absence of hard models, rules of thumb have tended to govern a field in which it's more important for a program to be useful than to be totally correct
abstract: No theories of software reliability have been developed that are as powerful or as widely accepted as theories of hardware reliability. Some software specialists even question whether there is any practical meaning in such concepts as mean time to failure or mean time between failures; they argue that the distribution of software failures over time may have no mean value. Many workers therefore speak only of error rates, or of the estimated total bugs remaining. It is widely believed that even the most thoroughly debugged software still has glitches. The only vital requirement is that the program be useful, although not necessarily 100 percent correct.

articleTitle: Automotive electronics: Detroit bets on electronics to stymie Japan: Programmable controllers, robots, lasers, and microwave detectors maintain quality on U.S. auto makers' production and assembly fines
abstract: In Detroit's all-out war against imported cars, particularly Japanese models, quality has become synonymous with survival. “Final assembly by warranty” and “let the dealer finish the car” are no longer viable. “Get it right the first time” is today's mandate, and in striving for quality on production and assembly lines, U.S. car makers are turning increasingly to electronic devices and systems.

A new microelectronic implantable device, improved artificial arms and legs, and advanced large diagnostic scanners were among the outstanding developments as medical electronics continued its rapid strides forward.

articleTitle: Power/energy: I. Efficient devices/systems: Utilities explore new means to cut energy losses during transmission and distribution
abstract: With electric power demand either slowing in growth or leveling off recently in many areas of the United States, utilities are “entrenching in the present,” says Kenneth Klein, deputy director of the office of Electric Energy Systems Division in the Federal Department of Energy. Economic downturns and consumer conservation contributed to the falloff in demand. As a result, many utilities trimmed their long-term research and development budgets, and virtually all showed interest in cutting energy losses during transmission and distribution. The funds for many research projects come mainly from the DOE and the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) of Palo Alto, Calif.

articleTitle: Power/energy: Satellite control of electric power distribution: A single satellite can manage loads, automate distribution, and read all power meters from coast to coast
abstract: A single satellite could cycle electric water heaters on and off in homes and factories, activate switchgear in power distribution stations, and even read electric meters - all over the United States. These and other forms of load and operations management could be commonplace in five years, if only a fraction of the country's 2000 utilities cooperated in sponsoring the satellite. Satellite monitoring and control of the U.S. electrical distribution network would be both effective and economical.

articleTitle: Automotive electronics: All-electronic dashboards coming: CRT, liquid crystal, and electroluminescent displays show promise for large-area, multifunction driver information systems in future cars
abstract: Most electronic displays in today's production cars are either extra-cost options on "inexpensive" models or standard equipment on high-priced, luxury models. Like the less-expensive mechanical and electromechanical displays they replace, the electronic devices tend to be both single-function units, such as digital clocks, and fixed-format units, such as bar graphs. In these modes, the displays are not being used to their full capabilities. This restrictive environment is destined to change.

abstract: The number vi home applicationes Incorporatin microprocessor control continues to grow. articleTitle: Spectral lines: The density (and frailty) of our history
abstract: Recently, when a writer who undertook an assignment to review the early history of the transistor approached one of the companies that had been deeply involved, he found to his dismay that little primary documentation had survived. Instead, he had to content himself with copies of press releases from the firm's public relations department. Thus, an important record of accomplishments by the company and its technical personnel was lost to posterity.

articleTitle: Computers: Fast graphics use parallel techniques: Designers of computer graphics systems exploit parallel processing to provide the speed needed for interactive performance
abstract: The main strength of computer graphics is in its ability to exploit the massive parallel processing capacity of human vision — the capacity to perceive almost instantly complex visual patterns. However, until recently, the graphics displays have generally been prepared serially by the computer hardware. Because of the large volume of information to be computed in three-dimensional graphics, this has meant long processing times, a problem not critical for scientific and entertainment applications, but serious for the interactive, real-time systems used in computer-assisted design and in real-time simulations, in these systems, the main trend now is toward the development of parallel processing hardware that can dramatically decrease processing times.

Leading the blind: A miniature TV camera and a stimulator belt are part of a “talking” experimental microprocessor-based system that is being tested as a walking aid for blind persons. The prototype apparatus, being developed at the Smith-Kettlewell Institute of Visual Sciences in San Francisco, recognizes obstacles, describes them in synthesized speech, and indicates their direction and distance through signals to a 16-position electromechanical belt worn by the blind person.

articleTitle: Best bits: Applications of microprocessors: Smart small-craft radar
abstract: Until now commercial srna tl-boat radar systems have disolayed targets as blips of light on a rotating-beam, monochromatic cathode-ray-tube screen, with the blips fading until the electron beam refreshed them on the next revolution. A new microprocessor-based X-band radar system developed by Western Marine Electronics Co. of Seattie, Wash., eliminate the fading problem; displays the targets and range circles in different colors; gives the coordinates of selected targets; warns when targets get too close; and permits additional display monitors to be located throghout the boat. The microorocessor (Zilog's Z80) also eliminates about half the circuitry usually found in comparable marine radar systems.

articleTitle: Nuclear power: INPO: Utilities create their own policeman: The burden of helping demonstrate the nuclear industry's commitment to safety is on the Institute of Nuclear Power Operations
abstract: The utilities, the regulators, and everyone connected with the nuclear industry in the United States point to the creation of the Institute of Nuclear Power Operations (INPO), now a year and a half old. as evidence of the industry's commitment to safety. Organized in Atlanta mainly to establish industrywide standards for the operation of nuclear power plants and to ensure that the utilities meet those standards, this first attempt at self-policing by the industry has support (100 percent of the utilities operating nuclear plants in the U.S. belong), big plans (an evaluation of every nuclear station in the U.S. is to be completed by the end of this year), and plenty of money (all utilities belonging paid their share of the $11 million 1980 budget and are expected to contribute $17.4 million in the first quarter of 1981). But, as might be expected with a young organization, potentially serious problems exist.

articleTitle: Consumer electronics: The continuing quest for 3-D television: The solution lies in deceiving the eye; viewers must envision a realistic image where a planar one exists
abstract: The goal oi reproducing pictures and scenes as human eyes perceive them has eluded engineers since the days of the silent movies. The addition of a third dimension, to create life-like events, has been regarded mostly as an optics problem: To solve it, work the lenses so the eye is fooled by an optical illusion. The methods have never beengood; most have required the viewerto wear glasses with polarized lenses, which makes for an awkward setting for entertainment. Some engineers say digital electronics and real-time processing computers may change that.

articleTitle: III. Management faces the facts: Damaging accidents are possible
abstract: The accident at TMI and its aftermath has hit most utility managers like a bucket of ice water in the face. Many were roused from a complacency that had led them to believe that serious accidents just could not happen. The NRC had required so many safeguards, they felt, that their plants were foolproof. Two years later, there is a growing awareness that accidents can indeed happen, that utilities cannot rely on the NRC to ensure safety, and that utilities must develop their own expertise to cope with emergencies.

abstract: In the U.S., there are 73 commercial nuclear reactors in operation. Eighty-three more are in various stages of construction, and construction permits are being sought for 12 others. The numbers are essentially the same as before the TMI accident, though a few plants have been canceled, and chances are good that nearly all of the proposed plants will eventually be licensed to operate.

abstract: Progress toward metric conversion in the U.S., although less advanced than some would prefer, is occurring even without an enunciated national plan. articleTitle: Computers: Higher densities for disk memories: Despite rumors of their impending demise, disk memories are alive and well, and with good reason
abstract: Ten years ago, disk memory technology was widely thought to be exhausted, with no promise of significant future increases in bit density, and bound to be obsoleted soon by the new semiconductor memories. Yet, disks have defied all efforts since then to dislodge them as the dominant computer mass-storage devices. Their bit density has increased several hundred times in the past decade — as fast a growth rate as the more publicized semiconductor memories of recent years — and it may increase almost as fast in the 1980s. However, disk technology today is indeed straining the limits of recording on particulate media — a coating of gamma type iron oxide — although the fundamental magnetic limits are still several orders of magnitude away. Further density increases require improvements in recording media, read/write heads, and encoding methods. Nevertheless, rigid disk memories will probably have at least 108 bits per square inch by the late 1980s. The increased density will be obtained by further exploiting thin-film read/write heads, and particulate (iron oxide) recording media. Thin-film media or perpendicular recording may trigger new density increases by the late 1980s or the mid 1990s, depending largely on marketing considerations.

abstract: A recurring nightmare for reliability engineers might be one in which they spend weeks searching for the cause of certain failures, only to have the cause become obvious to the first unqualified person who comes along.

abstract: The market for small-business systems changed dramatically last year as manufacturers introduced the first wireless portable terminals — hand-held terminals that communicate with host computers via radio. At the same time, the makers of personal computers began to compete with IBM and the scores of other experienced companies in this market.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: The anonymity of mice and men
abstract: You may recall Spectrum's Amazing Micro-Mouse Maze Contest. It was conceived in late 1976 and announced in May 1977. The objective was to build a thinking mouse, one that could find its way through a maze, the configuration of which had been kept secret until race time, learn through its mistakes and, in subsequent runs, solvethe mazewithout error.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Science, technology, and the Government
abstract: The role of U.S. scientists and engineers in administrations prior to President Reagan's has surely been vicissitudinous. For example, Richard M. Nixon abolished the separate post of science advisor to the White House, a post that was established by Dwight D. Eisenhower, in its place, Mr. Nixon asked the director of the National Science Foundation to double as Presidential advisor. That was hardly an ideal arrangement, and yet it did not seem to inspire as much criticism from the technical community and informed public as has President Reagan's apparent failure to recognize the importance of technology.

articleTitle: Tools for controlling quality: What is done prior to production, as well as thereafter, is as important as the production process itself in ensuring the quality of products
abstract: In the Middle Ages, skilled craftsmen worked long years as apprentices under the watchful eyes of journeymen and masters before they were prepared to produce quality products. But with the introduction of interchangeable parts by Eli Whitney at the beginning of the 19th century, new methods of quality control were required. First piece-part measurements, then inspections and statistical sampling techniques, were introduced. By World War II, modern methods of quality control were established, and in the past four decades these have changed relatively little.

articleTitle: Automotive electronics; Electronic fuel injection: Diesels are next: Auto producers turn to electronics to meet emission standards for diesel engines. It's tougher going compared with gasoline engines
abstract: Most automobile gasoline engines today are equipped with electronic controls and exhaust aftertreatment to optimize fuel economy and meet emission requirements. Today's automobile diesel engines, on the other hand, use 25 to 50 percent less fuel than gasoline engines and meet diesel emission standards without electronic controls or exhaust aftertreatment. But, as more stringent diesel emission standards evolve in the next several years, electronic controls will be needed to refine diesel performance. The first such application will be for fuel injection control. Diesel exhaust aftertreatment, now under study, will come later.

articleTitle: Technology transfer: Technology: Dichotomous tool: It can foster trade, but threaten security. Current U.S. policy has tightened controls on exports to the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe
abstract: The Kama River truck factory in the Soviet Union is one of the World's largest industrial complexes. The United States and Western Europe contributed to its design, construction, and operations with shipments of equipment and transfer of technology from 1971 through 1975. The value of shipments from the U.S. alone, including an IBM computer to control the factory's foundry operations, totaled $355 million. When troops of the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan in 1979, trncks supporting the Soviet military units were identified as products of the Kania River factory. in recent months, Kama River trucks have supported the military maneuvers of Soviet troops near the Polish border.

articleTitle: II. The human side: Training and tools to help the operator
abstract: A clogged demineralizer line that caused a turbine to trip, a leaky pressurizer that disguised a loss of coolant accident, and a valve that stuck open - these were the equipment problems that triggered the accident at Three Mile Island. Since that accident, however, study after study has observed that if the automatic safety systems had been untouched by human hands, these hardware failures might not have led to the calamity at TMI. The real damage at TMI was caused by unprepared operators, confused by both inadequate training and poor control room diagnostic aids, who inadvertently, but systematically, checkmated every automatic safety system until the core began inciting. What the accident at TMI showed was that ill-prepared operators could make things worse.

articleTitle: Sociotechnology: Nuclear weapons monitoring: The international community is desperately trying to devise schemes and systems to discourage proliferation. It could be an unending struggle
abstract: When Israel last month bombed an Iraqi atomic reactor, later contending that the facility could be used in the manufacture of nuclear weapons, the prospect of nuclear arms proliferation among nations that are not superpowers hit home hard. But the controversial Israeli action merely shifted the world's attention from one tense global theater to another.

articleTitle: IV. NRC's new zeal, a face-lift, and increased regulation
abstract: If the TMI accident hit utility managers like ice water, it was no less shocking to the regulators in the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Post-TMI study groups sharply criticized the agency's personnel, structure, and pre-TMI laxities. Critics asked: Why did the NRC not strictly enforce compliance with its safety regulations? Why was there no strong leadership directing the agency's priorities? Why did the agency fail to examine every abnormal operating event and disseminate the information throughout the nuclear industry? Some of the questions have been brought into the courtroom. General Public Utilities, the owner of the crippled TMI reactor, has filed suit against the NRC for $4 billion alleging inadequate oversight of safety. GPU charges that the TMI accident might not have happened if the NRC had told the utility about an incident at the Davis-Besse reactor in Ohio, during which a sequence of events almost identical to those that triggered TMI occurred. (The incident at the Davis-Besse reactor, owned jointly by the Toledo Edison Co. and the Cleveland Electric Illuminating Co., occurred at low power and did not progress as far as the TMI accident.)

articleTitle: Data communications: Local data nets: Untying the office knot: Establishing standards for accessing local data networks may facilitate intra-office communications
abstract: Business communications are headed for spectacular expansion in this decade as companies draw up plans to convert their headquarters into "electronic offices." Already, some of the larger manufacturers of equipment for these offices are offering communications networks that allow word processors, intelligent terminals, magnetic disk units, minicomputers, and the like to communicate with one another via software protocols. When VLSI becomes predominant, the way will be clear for inexpensive high-bandwidth communications between office equipment in a limited area. Each office building will then become a local data communications network. The electronic office will have come of age. The ultimate goal is to efficiently link the local networks with remote inter-city networks (Fig. 1).

articleTitle: Spectral lines: A measure of class
abstract: The other day, Marjorie Damon went to the Wellesley, Mass., town dump. Ms. Damon is a columnist for the Wellesley Townsman, a weekly newspaper having a circulation of some 7800 readers. Going to the town dump is something of a tradition in New England, for it is there that one catches up on news of the neighbors, and engages in caucuses regarding agenda items for the annual town meeting.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: IEEE examines its heritage
abstract: Just two years from now the IEEE will celebrate the 100th anniversary of its founding. If we intend to have a cake, it will have to be a big one, and the time to start bringing together the ingredients is now.

'Either it's reliable or it's not' is a commonly expressed view of the lay public as they think of their own automobiles and television sets. Even engineers, when wearing their "consumer hats," may lapse into temporary support of this simplistic belief. Unexpected failures can impair one's ability to think calmly and logically.

articleTitle: Consumer electronics: Shrinking products pose problems: Small, well-designed audio and video units capture the buyer's fancy but challenge human-factors engineers
abstract: Consumer electronics companies are advertising a television set that is “smaller than a paperback book,” video recorders “light enough to sit on eggs,” and typewriters only slightly larger “than an eyeglass case.” Electronics equipment for the typical office and home is getting smaller.

articleTitle: Solid state/energy: Solar-cell systems that work: In applications from irrigation pumps to village power systems, photovoltaic installations are now producing electricity economically
abstract: A national park in Utah derives all its electricity from silicon solar cells. A house in Massachusetts - far from the Sun Belt - draws at least SO percent of its electrical needs from the sun via a photovoltaic array on its roof. At an 80-acre farm in Nebraska, a photovoltaic system pumps water for irrigation in the summer and fans air for crop drying in the fall. The three solar-cell installations have this in common: they are working examples of the major categories of photovoltaic applications of the future - perhaps the near future.

articleTitle: Computers: Speech recognition: Turning theory to practice: New ICs have brought the requisite computer power to speech technology; an evaluation of equipment shows where it stands today
abstract: Ten years ago speech scientists were predicting that automatic dictation and other sophisticated applications of electronic speech recognition would not be possible in this century, if ever. Today the outlook appears more optimistic. Such applications may be commercial by 2000 - perhaps earlier.

articleTitle: Solid state: Bistable optical devices promise subpicosecond switching: Extensive research in materials and phenomena could lead to their ultimate use in optical communications, despite high power dissipation
abstract: A new type of optical element - a bistable optical device that exhibits two distinct states of transmission of light through it - is being developed in several laboratories. With its extraordinary range of optical signal processing capabilities, it could become a key component in future high-speed optical communications repeaters, as well as in terminai equipment, data communication systems, and systems for the direct optical processing of visual images.

articleTitle: Power semiconductors: Switching lots of watts at high speeds: State-of-the-art development yields solid-state devices capable of handling over 10 million watts
abstract: Today the frontier in power electronics lies in high-frequency switching applications, such as variable-frequency ac motor drives and solid-state lamp ballasts. Several new power devices have been developed in the semiconductor industry to meet this challenge. In particular, power MOSFETs capable of efficient high-frequency switching at several kilowatts have been announced by many companies. The operational ratings of these devices should grow rapidly and, although commercial power MOSFETs have been available for only three years, it is already clear that they will displace the bipolar transistor in many high-frequency applications. Several other power devices under development at various laboratories are also expected to find a niche in the high-frequency spectrum.

articleTitle: Risk assessment: Probing the question of technology-induced risk: What risk is and how we think about it are analyzed by establishing a framework of real and perceived effects
abstract: In the first of two articles on risk assessment and management, the author explores what constitutes risk. A second article in the December Spectrum will examine questions of regulation and management of risk.

articleTitle: Risk assessment: Choosing and managing technology-induced risk: How much risk should we choose to live with? How should we assess and manage the risks we face?
abstract: This is the second of two articles on risk assessment. In the first, published last month, the author developed a framework for thinking about risk [Fig. 1]. In this framework, two processes - exposures and effects, at left in figure - act upon natural processes and human activites to produce some effect or change. The other two processes - perception and evaluation, at right in figure - act upon this change and develop some notion of risk through costs and benefits.

articleTitle: Solid state: Silicon sensors meet integrated circuits: The combination of sensing and circuit technology in monolithic form is making transducers cheaper and more versatile
abstract: Advances in silicon sensor technology are now permitting a merger of sensors and integrated circuits into “integrated sensors” - single silicon chips containing both sensors and circuitry. As a result, the transducer industry stands at a threshold that was crossed by the microelectronics industry in the early 1960s. The next several years will see an explosion of sensors and sensor applications. Silicon sensors will be introduced both in applications where costly hand-assembled devices were previously used and in those where sensors have been too expensive. Used in conjunction with microprocessors, sensors will increasingly contribute to improved system performance, with decreased part count and decreased cost.

articleTitle: Materials: Metallic glasses: Researchers are grappling with novel production techniques that would revolutionize transformer manufacturing
abstract: For two decades, researchers have been investigating metallic glasses , materials that can be magnetized easily and that have remarkably low magnetic losses. But mass-producing the glasses , or amorphous metals, as they are also called - requires the development of a totally new technology, and this has held back their large-scale applications. They are produced continuously in ribbons 20 to 50 micrometers thick, or about one tenth the thickness of the standard laminated steel used today in transformer cores [Fig. 1]. They are harder and also more sensitive to mechanical stresses than steel. Thus, novel transformer manufacturing techniques must be developed.

articleTitle: Military electronics: Electromagnetic pulses: Potential crippler: Three bombs, exploded in space over the U.S., could black out the nation, wipe out communications, and make computers useless
abstract: An international crisis is in progress. The Early Warning System alerts the North American AirDefense headquarters in Colorado that missiles have just been launched at the United States. Commanders immediately act to determine if the alert is real or a result of computer malfunction. In minutes, the alert is confirmed, and news of the attack is conveyed to the President.

articleTitle: Communications: Fiber-optic transducers: Sensing and control systems based on fiber-optic conversion of input variables into modulated light signals are in development
abstract: For more than a century, researchers have tried to improve ways of converting input variables into electric signals. Today there is a modest but growing effort going into a different kind of sensing: converting variables into light signals.

articleTitle: Data processing: Pattern recognition: A review: Optical techniques developed to discern military targets are being studied for industrial and commercial applications
abstract: Optical pattern-recognition systems " systems that use optical interference to process incoming signals " have long attracted attention because of their highly parallel operation and high speed. Until now, most research in the United States has concentrated on military applications, such as missile guidance and electronic warfare. However, although the emphasis remains primarily on military applications, recent advances in optical system components, system architecture, and pattern-recognition algorithms suggest development of systems with potential commercial applications in robotics, automated product inspection, and other civilian fields.

articleTitle: How parts fail: A fundamental explanation for any part failure exists, and it's up to the failure analyst to find the cause with modern sleuthing
abstract: An understanding of how semiconductor and other electronic parts fail is essential to improving the reliability of devices as well as that of the systems in which they are used. Such failure analyses help identify device failure modes, mechanisms, and stress factors that influence degradation.

articleTitle: Aerospace: Navstar: The all-purpose satellite: The military sees Navstar as a way of keeping wide-ranging forces on target, and potential civilian users are showing interest too
abstract: By the turn of the century, a single system “ Navstar ” may serve most of the United States' global navigation and position-determination needs. Although, right now, it's a military system, the Navstar Global Positioning System (GPS) has shown its worth in a variety of civilian uses: maritime, aviation, and space. If Navstar is eventually adopted for U.S. civilian use, it will provide for the first time a common system for all classes of users, and it may reverse the proliferation of special-purpose navigation and positioning systems.

articleTitle: Solid state: Fast electron-beam lithography: High blanking speeds may make this new system a serious challenger in producing submicrometer ICs
abstract: For the first time, electron-beam lithography may become competitive with optical methods, the leading production process today for making integrated circuits. The step that could make this possible is an electron-beam lithography system developed at Hewlett-Packard that is potentially many times faster than previous such machines for making ICs through direct writing on wafers or generating high-precision masks.

articleTitle: Computers: From Eniac to Univac: As inventors, Eckert and Mauchly were clear successes, but as entrepreneurs they had some difficult times
abstract: In the electronics boom that followed World War II, some scientists and engineers preferred the advantages of universities and large industrial research organizations, and some sought success as entrepreneurs. Of those, a number succeeded in business while others failed, but all who tried quickly learned the same lesson: their toughest problems were those of business and commerce, not of the technology they were trying to develop.

articleTitle: Computers: A new breed: The software engineer: As more and better software designers are needed, universities and industry are under pressure to establish programs to train them
abstract: As computers in general and microcomputers in particular become an inexorable part of more and more new equipment, a new type of engineer is growing in importance. Bearing the title “software engineer,” he or she is part programmer and part systems-hardware and -software design engineer, among other things.

articleTitle: Southern California Edison bets on energy alternatives
abstract: One of the largest utilities in the United States, the Southern California Edison Co., wants the future now. And it is on its way to getting it. Before this year is out, it expects to begin operating in the Mojave Desert a 10-megawatt solar-thermal generating plant, the first to be run by an electric utility and the largest such project ever attempted in the world.

abstract: Without warning, the predawn stillness at the reactor facility is interrupted by a cacophony of alarms, lights, shouted orders, and frantic activity. articleTitle: Education: Engineering education: Coping with the crisis: Government, industry, and academic leaders meet to target solutions to the ominous decline in the academic environment
abstract: The economic health of the United States depends increasingly on the fruits of engineering technology. But the educational system that supplies engineers is eroding.

articleTitle: Computers: The computer graphics revolution: Slowly but surely, new software and hardware are making a reality of graphics specialists' dreams
abstract: Computer graphics is beginning to transform the way a large part of the data-processing industry operates. New software and hardware developed over the past several years have made practicable the accurate representation of three-dimensional objects of great complexity. This new capability, using computers of reasonable size and cost, has opened a widening field of applications.

articleTitle: Computer design: the microkids and the hardy boys: an inside look at how a maverick team from data general `rescued” the company by designing a competitive 32-bit superminicomputer in record time
abstract: In the fall of 1978 a journalist in his early 30s, Tracy Kidder, went on a sailing trip with a crew of strangers, among them an engineer named Tom West. During a storm off Maine, Mr. Kidder learned that Mr. West was, as another of their crew put it, “a good man in a storm.” The harder the wind blew and the more dangerous the conditions, the happier and more competent Mr. West became; crisis appeared to be his natural milieu.

articleTitle: Lessons from NASA: Design reviews, failure analysis, and redundancy are favored over predictions and life testing for spacecraft success
abstract: Spacecraft differ from other products of technology in several critical respects. They are exposed to hostile environments unlike any on earth. They cannot be repaired once they are launched. Production of a particular craft has been limited to one or at most a few models. The designs challenge the state of the art and use the latest hardware, which must be proved for the space environment by thorough testing.

articleTitle: Watchdog for nuclear development: Technology can help monitor civilian uses of nuclear energy while discouraging military applications
abstract: At a time when nuclear proliferation seems a growing threat to world peace, many countries are supporting technical efforts to monitor the constructive uses of nuclear, energy to help ensure that nuclear materials and technology are not diverted to weapons use. Recover (for REmote Continual VERification) is an experimental system designed to transmit data automatically from sensors at nuclear sites around the world to the headquarters of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) in Vienna, Austria. The system was developed under the auspices of the IAEA in a program initiated by the U.S. Arms Control and Disarmament Agency (ACDA).

articleTitle: Ethics: Five ethical dilemmas: Compare your own responses with those of your colleagues who responded to Spectrum's survey
abstract: John, an engineer at a components house, is working on a NASA contract and designs a component critical to a life-support system. It surpasses NASA's specifications and tests, and John is informed that he will receive a substantial bonus at a company dinner later in the year to reward him for his contribution. He is aware that there are conditions that will cause his component to fail, but it appears from NASA's original specifications that such conditions will never arise. Later, John discovers that the conditions will indeed occur in the missions planned by NASA. He immediately calls his superior, who stops production of the component and informs NASA. Loss of pride and money for the company and John ensue. He doesn't get a bonus. But, clearly, it was the only ethical thing to do; acting otherwise would have caused a man's death.

articleTitle: Communications: Getting set for direct-broadcast satellites: Three different technical approaches vie for FCC approval; here a generic system is examined
abstract: Direct broadcasting of television signals from a satellite to home TV receivers was envisioned some 35 years ago when Arthur C. Clark, a pioneer in satellite communications, broached the idea of putting communications satellites into geostationary orbit. The vision of direct-broadcast-satellite (DBS) television is close to reality today, so close that the main question no longer is whether such a satellite can be put into orbit - one or more will be out there by 1985. The critical question today is which DBS technical characteristics will give the best television reception.

On October 8, President Ronald Reagan issued a major policy statement on nuclear power. In doing so, he sought to reverse what a preinauguration energy task force had characterized as the Carter Administration's policy of “benign neglect” toward nuclear power. Specifically, the President's statement outlined steps designed to rescue the nuclear industry from its current doldrums, caused largely by lingering doubts about reactor safety following the accident at the Three Mile Island reactor, coupled with decreasing U.S. demand for electricity and escalating reactor costs. This offered a more favorable view of those advanced developments that nuclear proponents see as vital to the long-term future of nuclear power - that is, the reprocessing of commercial nuclear fuels and the development of the plutonium breeder reactor.

articleTitle: Lessons from the military: Applications, environments, and servicemen pose reliability challenges not found in commerce or industry
abstract: Reliability in military systems is complicated by many factors not usually encountered in commercial or industrial applications. Among them are the following constraints: • Military applications often require higher performance. To get it, designers must use advanced or revolutionary technology before the reliability of that technology has been proved. Nonmilitary systems, by contrast, are usually state-of-the-art, or evolutionary, products with a proven record of reliability. • Military system designers are often required to create a “perfect” design at an early stage. Nonmilitary system designers tend to use iterative approaches, in which they make many small changes to solve problems as they arise. • Military systems generally operate in harsh environments that have proved difficult to simulate under test conditions. The environments may include extremes of temperature, vibration, mechanical shock, humidity, or corrosive agents (such as sea water), as well as electromagnetic interference and nuclear radiation. The electromagnetic environment alone may have up to 100 different signals broadcast by enemy jamming systems or friendly forces. Experience has shown that some equipment in the field is only about one third as reliable as it was during final testing by the manufacturer. • The servicemenwho operate military systemsmaybe unusually error-prone. In the chaos of battle they are subjectto great stress, with accompanying lapses in performance. • The armed services are chronicallyshort of experienced operators and maintenance personnel in many areas, as well as reliability engineers. The services are confronted by chronically high turnover rates in personnel. • Manufacturers cannot always guarantee the reliability of spare parts or the adequacy of maintenance once the systemis in the field; some systemsmay be repaired with either unspecified parts or parts from various manufacturers, since the services are required by law to buy spare parts through competitivebids. • Military-gradedevicescost more than comparable commercial or industrial devices. They require specialmanufacturing, documantition, and testing procedures to ensure reliability and uniform quality. • Military procurement engineershave only minimal leverage in the semiconductorindustry. Military-grade integrated circuitsaccount for less than 10 percent of the industry's dollar sales, and they have not offered as stable a market as commerical items.

articleTitle: Aerospace: Shuttle firsts put to the test: After its near-perfect maiden flight, Columbia needs fine tuning for a trip that will highlight its remote arm and its first payload
abstract: Ten years of intricate development had ended in electrifying success. The world's first Space Shuttle had made it home to Edwards Air Force Base in California as effortlessly as any other airline shuttle. The Columbia had shown in a two-and-a-half-day flight from Cape Canaveral, Fla., last April 12 through 14 that it could be expected to carry payloads and workers into space and return safely to earth.

articleTitle: Communications: Postal automation: It can be done: The toughest task is to integrate the technology into a system that is archaic, unwieldy, and a victim of its own inertia
abstract: Despite the rapid development of electronic data transmission, there will be a need for a conventional postal system for a long time to come. The convenience and cheapness of letters will not easily be equaled by electronic mail. Yet, the present United States postal system does not provide the speed and reliability of delivery that the public has a right to expect.

articleTitle: Reliability test procedures: LSI circuits: Fault models make high-volume testing practical
abstract: The testing of large-scale-integrated circuits is a major factor in the cost of producing such digital devices as memory chips and microprocessors. Manufacturers could test earlier small- and medium-scale-integrated devices cheaply and exhaustively ― testing every possible state that the circuits could take up ― but they cannot do the same with LSI and very large-scale-integrated devices, because of the awesome number of states. For example, a 4096-bit random-access memory can have a total number of states, or combinations, of 2 raised to the 4096th power. With current test equipment operating at 10 megahertz, it would take an astronomical amount of time to test for every memory combination.

articleTitle: I. Engineering changes: New and improved systems and hardware
abstract: In the wake of the TMI. accident, the popular press has focused on the need for better operating procedures, better-trained operators, and improved management attitudes, but major changes are also being made in the equipment and systems of nuclear plants. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission's TMI. Action Plan (NUREG-0660 and 0737) details these new requirements and lists numerous engineering fixes to be made. These, as well as nontechnical items in the plan, arise principally from recommendations in the reports of three groups - the President's Commission on the Accident at Three Mile Island, the NRC-sponsored Special Inquiry Group, and the NRC's own Lessons Learned Task Force.

articleTitle: New product application: Microprocessor-controlled D-size plotter is sheet-fed, automates color and line-width selection
abstract: The HP 7580A plotter incorporates a “micro-grip” drive that moves sheets of the plotting medium in one direction over an airfoll-shaped bed, while the pen carriage operates in the perpendicular direction. The large-format plotter operates with paper, vellum, or polyester film. The plotter can be programmed for up to eight colors or line widths.

articleTitle: Solid state: The 64-Rkb RAM teaches a VLSI lessen: Solutions to the problems in developing 64-kb dynamic RAMs will hasten the arrival of new VLSI memory technology
abstract: When the first 64-kb dynamic RAMs built in the United States arrived recently on the market, they were halled as the bridge between LSI and VLSI memory chips-but what was also significant is that RAM makers had taken three years longer than they anticipated to deliver the new chips. Some industry observers raised questions, moreover, about whether the chips had circuit problems that rendered them less competitive than Japanese counterparts, and whether optimally designed 64-kb dynamic RAMs were still several years away.

articleTitle: How systems differ: Telephone system: Electronic switching, redundancy, and automatic recovery reduce outages
abstract: Telephone customers expect and usually obtain good quality service at any time under any condition. This high degree of availability is met even though any given telephone call involves numerous pieces of equipment. The major elements in a local call are the equipment at a customer's location, the wire pair connecting the customer to the local switching system, and the switching system itself. For toll calls, the local switch in a system is interconnected in a network of other switching and transmission systems. Failure anywhere in the physically distributed network can cause failure to originate a call, failure to complete the call to the called party, or unexpected cutoff.

articleTitle: Careers: We look at ourselves: The researcher: Driven by the thrill of discovery, researchers seek to contribute to society and to enhance their images among peers
abstract: Researchers in electrotechnology come in many sizes and personalities and with many interests. But if they have one common characteristic, it is an insatiable desire to understand. Whether the object of their study is a phenomenon, device, system, design, production technique, or mathematical theory, they stick with it until they have satisfied their curiosity.

A number of leading electronics companies in the United States are beginning to involve production workers in the effort to improve the quality and reliability of their products. They are borrowing techniques developed over the last 20 years in Japan, techniques in turn based on American social science theories. Unlike schemes tried previously in this country - such as the Zero Defects movement, which relied on individual worker motivation — the newly introduced ideas are based on worker committees called Quality Circles, after the Japanese Quality Control Circles (QCCs). These identify production and design problems and suggest means of solving them.
